scope: These notes distinguish Mitchell’s interviews, Nash’s recollections and critical interpretations. The Joni Mitchell Library hosts material originally published elsewhere; hosting is not authorship or independent corroboration. No new audio analysis or biographical deductions are asserted.

entries.description: Mitchell resisted the search for concealed meanings in “All I Want.” In the interview archived by her website, she described it as having more bite than many of her early songs and insisted that its meaning was in the words themselves.

sourceLabels.https://jonimitchell.com/library/view.cf: Joni Mitchell interview · Joni Mitchell Library archive

entries.question: Which words feel most direct to you when you take Mitchell’s plain-speaking approach?

entries.description: A 2021 New York Post article, archived in the Joni Mitchell Library, reads “My Old Man” as a portrait of domestic happiness with Graham Nash without the need for a marriage certificate.

sourceLabels.https://jonimitchell.com/library/view.cf: New York Post (2021) · Joni Mitchell Library archive

entries.description: In an interview preserved in the Joni Mitchell Library, Mitchell explained that poverty had forced her to give up her daughter for adoption. The accompanying article identifies that daughter, Kilauren, as the child in “Little Green.”

sourceLabels.https://jonimitchell.com/library/view.cf: Interview and accompanying article · Joni Mitchell Library archive

entries.description: Mitchell’s recollection of meeting Cary Raditz begins with an explosion. She told the Los Angeles Times that a stove blew him out of a restaurant doorway; her reaction was that she had to meet him.

sourceLabels.https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-ar: Joni Mitchell interview · Los Angeles Times

entries.description: Reviewing the album in 1971, Rolling Stone’s Timothy Crouse heard the title song as a concentration of pain and an unusually private piece of writing.

sourceLabels.https://jonimitchell.com/library/view.cf: Timothy Crouse · Rolling Stone (1971), via Joni Mitchell Library

entries.question: Does the song feel private to you in the way Crouse described, and what in it gives you that impression?

entries.description: Timothy Crouse’s 1971 Rolling Stone review frames this song around a reversal: its narrator has left a relationship, is travelling west by jet, and now regrets leaving. The description follows the review’s reading of the story rather than treating it as a verified episode in Mitchell’s life.

sourceLabels.https://jonimitchell.com/library/view.cf: Timothy Crouse · Rolling Stone (1971), via Joni Mitchell Library

entries.question: How does the narrator’s regret change your understanding of the journey?

entries.description: Mitchell gave a direct account of “River” to the Los Angeles Times: regret after a relationship ends, and loneliness at Christmas. She thought that seasonal loneliness helped explain why the song connected with so many people.

sourceLabels.https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-ar: Joni Mitchell interview · Los Angeles Times

entries.question: How does the Christmas setting affect the sense of regret for you?

entries.description: Graham Nash remembered Mitchell writing at the piano in the Laurel Canyon house they shared. A New York Post article archived in the Joni Mitchell Library places “A Case of You” among the songs he saw her write there.

sourceLabels.https://jonimitchell.com/library/view.cf: New York Post (2021) · Joni Mitchell Library archive
